# 2. Data sources and sample description

We use farm-level microdata from the Ghana Living Standards Survey (GLSS) Waves 6 (2012/13) and 7 (2016/17). Both waves are repeated cross-sections drawn via a two-stage design (enumeration areas, then households). Following the GLSS documentation, [@Tsiboe2020] consolidate the raw files to a farmer-level dataset that has supported several analyses of agricultural productivity in Ghana [21], [22], [23], [25], [26]. Our study focuses on crop farmers, trimming yield outliers by keeping observations with yields (kg/ha) between the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles within survey round × crop. As shown in Table 1, the final sample comprises `r fmt_num(objs$sample$n_pooled, 0)` farm operators cultivating at least one of the following: banana, beans, cashew, cassava, citrus, cocoa, coconut, cocoyam, cotton/kenaf, maize, millet, oil-palm, groundnut, plantain, potato, rice, sorghum, yam, sugarcane, tomato, pepper, okra, onion, eggplant, and other minor crops.

The consolidated files do not include a pre-built financial-inclusion module, so we reconstruct credit and financial-service indicators directly from the original GLSS questionnaires. Using preserved enumeration-area, household, and member IDs, we extract items from Part B, Section 12a (credit, banking, use of financial services, and insurance) and merge them to the farmer-level file. Table S0 in the appendix documents, for each round, the source variables, the question wording, the response options, and their mapping to the analysis variables; Tables 2 and 3 report their incidence.

We define credit use at the individual level as the conjunction of three conditions in the twelve months preceding the interview: the person applied for a loan from a financial institution (GLSS6 `s12aq7`, GLSS7 `s12aq7`); the application was granted (GLSS6 `s12aq8`, GLSS7 `s12aq8a`–`s12aq8c`); and a positive loan amount was recorded (`s12aq10` in both rounds). All three are required. The survey's skip pattern makes them close to equivalent in practice, because an amount is elicited only for a granted application, but the indicator is a conjunction, not a disjunction, and a household that applied and was refused is a non-user however the question is read. Our preferred treatment is a household-level indicator equal to 1 if (i) the farm operator, (ii) the operator's spouse, (iii) an operator's child, or (iv) any other household member satisfies that criterion. Aggregating to the household rather than the operator reflects the pooling of liquidity within farm households: a loan taken by a spouse relaxes the same constraint on the same farm, and the frontier the analysis characterises is the household's technology, not the operator's borrowing record.

By this definition, `r fmt_pct(objs$credit$share_hh, 2)` of sample households used credit. Component shares are `r fmt_pct(objs$credit$share_self, 2)` operator, `r fmt_pct(objs$credit$share_spouse, 2)` spouse, and `r fmt_pct(objs$credit$share_member, 2)` other member. Criteria (i)–(iii) are not mutually exclusive, since a household may have both operator and spouse credit, so the components sum to more than the household rate; criterion (iv) is disjoint from the others by construction. Unless stated otherwise, “credit user(s)” refers to this household-level measure. The farmer-only variant, which counts only criterion (i), reclassifies `r fmt_pct(objs$credit$reclass_farmer_only, 2)` of the sample, in one direction only: it is a strict subset of the household measure, since no operator borrows in a household recorded as having no credit. Section 5 reports the estimates under both definitions.

Two features of the instrument bound what the indicator can measure. First, the two rounds do not code loan outcomes the same way: GLSS6 records a binary granted/not-granted, while GLSS7 adds a third status, “processing,” which the indicator treats as non-use because no loan has been disbursed. This affects `r fmt_pct(objs$credit$processing_share_glss7, 2)` of GLSS7 applicants and has no GLSS6 counterpart, so cross-round comparisons of approval are comparing a two-way split against a three-way one. Second, GLSS7 elicits status, source, purpose and collateral for up to three loans but records a single loan amount, so where an applicant reports several loans the amount cannot be attributed to a particular one; GLSS6, with one loan slot, has no such ambiguity. Loan amounts reported in Table 3 are CPI-deflated to 2016/17 cedis. Table S0 sets out the per-round source variables, question wording and response options in full.

The classification is insensitive to how the three conditions are combined. Requiring only that a positive amount be recorded, or only that an application be granted, reproduces the study indicator row for row, because the questionnaire elicits an amount only where an application succeeded. Relaxing the criterion to any loan application, whatever its outcome, raises the operator-level rate from `r fmt_pct(objs$credit$share_self, 2)` to `r fmt_pct(objs$credit$applied_share, 2)`, but that is a different construct: it counts households whose applications were refused or still pending alongside those that received funds.

Table 1 reports descriptive statistics of the pooled and credit-disaggregated samples, focusing on farmer, crop, and household characteristics. Female farmers account for `r tbl_pct("table1", "Female farmer (dummy)", 1, 0)` of the pooled sample and the average farmer is `r tbl_num("table1", "Age (years)", 1)` years old with a little over `r tbl_num("table1", "Education (years)", 1)` years of schooling. Mean household size is about `r tbl_num("table1", "Size (AE)", 1)` adult equivalents (AE) and the dependency ratio `r tbl_num("table1", "Dependency (ratio)", 1)`. Consistent with national statistics on smallholder farmers [@MoFA2017], farms in our sample averages less than `r fmt_num(ceiling(tbl_num("table1", "Land (ha)", 1)), 0)` ha (≈`r tbl_num("table1", "Land (ha)", 1)` ha), of which `r tbl_pct("table1", "Land owned (dummy)", 1, 0)` is owned, and crop diversification score is `r tbl_num("table1", "Crop diversification (index)", 1)` on our index.

Comparatively, credit users do not differ by household size or dependency ratios from non-users, but they are significantly younger (`r tbl_num("table1", "Age (years)", 3)` vs. `r tbl_num("table1", "Age (years)", 2)` years) and more educated (`r tbl_num("table1", "Education (years)", 3)` vs. `r tbl_num("table1", "Education (years)", 2)` years). Baseline per-hectare yields are statistically similar at 5% level for all crops except rice and yam (where non-users edge out users) and cocoyam and tomato (users outperform non-users). Additionally, credit access appears to be associated with increased hired labor employment and pesticide use, but not with other inputs. Moreover, over 2012–2017 fertilizer use among credit users increased by `r tbl_num("table1", "Fertilizer (Kg/ha)", 6)` kg/ha annually, while it remained statistically flat for non-users. Together, these statistics suggest largely uniform balance (and therefore, comparability) between users and non-users. Notwithstanding, the isolated imbalances between treated and control households justify our use of propensity score matching.
